text: be noted that marginal emissions rates are used in this analysis, which show zero-emissions generation sources on the margin on average 3 hours of the day. The load impacts modeled in this study are significant, increasing daytime load 10 or even 15 GW at times. These impacts would not be considered “marginal”, and therefore it is unlikely that for a given system build out there would be enough excess renewables available to meet such demand. However, if the system were to be built out to accommodate this load, with increased renewables and grid perhaps grid scale storage, then it is possible to significantly reduce emissions with these load shifts. As with other metrics (besides bill savings), results are quite similar across tariff design scenarios, with a slight reduction when moving from Full to Medium or Medium to Mild designs. 38 The difference between 2019 and 2030 is stark, as the load flexibility potential grows along with the marginal emissions differentials. This highlights the importance of ongoing modeling to understand the evolving end use loads on the grid and renewables generation and system emissions dynamics. While cooling loads provide the most flexibility in terms of effective shed or avoided cost metrics, the emissions metric highlights the benefits of year-round flexibility that EV charging, pool pumps, and water heating provides. Space heating load flexibility can also offer small but noticeable emissions savings, despite this end use not contributing as much to other metrics like effective shed. Figure 24.
